title: Franken Fran
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: Fran, an artificial girl built by the vanished surgeon Dr. Madaraki, carries on his medical work at a remote mansion in rural Japan. Patients come to her for cosmetic surgery, strength, popularity or even resurrection, and her radical operations keep them alive but often leave them grotesquely mutated. The episodic chapters are 'monkey's paw' stories that use body horror and black comedy to satirize the obsessions that drive people to her.
life_message: Life itself is to be preserved at any cost, while the story's satire suggests that vanity and greed bring their own monstrous results.

content.note: Graphic surgery, mutilation and mutation in most chapters; an assassin sister and a shapeshifter who mutilates Veronica (Wikipedia; Otaku USA review; AniList Gore, Body Horror).
Sustained body horror played for dark humor, e.g. a girl's head kept alive as a pet (Otaku USA review; AniList Body Horror 93, MU Dark Ambience).

AniList Nudity, Ero Guro and Yuri tags; MU Nudity and Ero-Guro; MangaDex 'suggestive'. A spoiler-tagged rape tag is low-ranked and voted down on MU. Not covered by Wikipedia or the review (to verify).
Gavrill is described as foul-mouthed (Wikipedia); level of profanity in the English edition to verify.
AniList and MU tag no drug use (to verify).
Patients' self-image obsessions and despair drive many chapters; quality of life is often destroyed (Wikipedia; AniList Body Horror, MU Social Commentary).
Radical cosmetic and enhancement procedures always backfire; satire rather than invitation.
Satire of beauty, popularity and wealth culture (Wikipedia; AniList Satire).

dominant: Transhumanism critiqued through body horror; life-at-any-cost ethics; black-comedy absurdism

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Fran and her sisters punish those who threaten the estate or hurt others, but most chapters turn on patients' private desires.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Fran operates outside law and medical licensing, answering only to her own oath.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to the Madaraki 'family' of creations is strong; sisters protect the estate.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Fran reveres her absent creator and Dr. Amatsuka; otherwise little rank theme.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Science replaces gods; Madaraki calls WWII a war to 'kill the gods' (Wikipedia).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Patients seek beauty and status; survival itself is Fran's supreme value.

folkways.japan: Ero-guro (erotic-grotesque) is an established strand of Japanese horror art, and the rural mansion setting and episodic monster-of-the-week format draw on that tradition, described here as context.

delivery.evidence: Episodic satire per sources; no review cited on whether it lectures (to verify).

personified.ideology: 'All lives must be saved, no matter the cost' (publisher blurb)

delivery.note: Each case lets vanity and greed produce grotesque results, so the satire works through outcomes rather than speeches.

winners_losers: Fran almost always 'wins' by keeping patients alive; greedy, vain and corrupt patients lose their old bodies and lives. The satire sympathizes with no one fully, though Fran's sincere care is played straight.
